In the gabbro the pla- gioclase is equigranular and clinopyroxene com- monly occurs as an interstitial constituent. Mi- cropegmatitic intergrowths of quartzofeldspathic material occasionally occur along some plagio- clase grain boundaries in both gabbro and do- lerite. In the leucogabbro, slight deuteric alter- ation of clinopyroxene into pale green amphibole (actinolite) is common along internal cleavages and grain boundaries. However, the amphibole does not occur as independent grains or entirely replace original minerals. Fe-Ti oxides occur as dispersed grains, locally with skeletal shapes. Geochemical characteristics suggest that the dolerites and the gabbro were derived from dis- crete parental magmas [6]. In terms of incompati- ble trace elements, the dolerites are correlative with tholeiitic units within upper stratigraphic units in the Deccan basalts. ke swarms occurring within the granulite terrain in central Kerala (west coast of India). Palaeomagnetic data show that the NNW-SSE leucogabbro dykes sampled are normally magnetised (D = 307 and I = -57), whereas most NW-SE dolerite dykes are reversely magnetised (D = 163 and I = 61). One dolerite dyke shows normal polarity. The present 4°Ar/39Ar isotope ages for dolerite dykes and previously reported K-Ar ages for leucogabbros suggest 81 + 2 Ma for acquisition of the leucogabbro directions and 69 + 1 Ma for acquisition of the reverse magnetic directions within the dolerites. Based on palaeomagnetic and isotopic age data, the dolerite dykes appears to represent feeder systems for the Deccan volcanic sequences. We suggest that the Deccan eruptions were widespread, and probably extended southward at least into central Kerala. The entire magmatic episode may have occurred between ca. 70 and 65 Ma (during the 31R period probably corresponding to the Cretaceous/Tertiary boundary). The leucogabbros may correspond to the 34N superchron and represent a plume-related magmatic episode precursory to the main volcanic event. These data suggest that an early intraplate plume tectonic setting (since ca. 80 Ma) preceded lithospheric thinning, asthenospheric upwelling and consequent mas

rala. The entire magmatic episode may have occurred between ca. 70 and 65 Ma (during the 31R period probably corresponding to the Cretaceous/Tertiary boundary). The leucogabbros may correspond to the 34N superchron and represent a plume-related magmatic episode precursory to the main volcanic event. These data suggest that an early intraplate plume tectonic setting (since ca. 80 Ma) preceded lithospheric thinning, asthenospheric upwelling and consequent massive flood volcanism during the period 70-65 Ma. This culminated in ocean-floor spreading between the Seychelles-Mascarene and continental India. I. Introduction Several Phanerozoic dyke swarms are exposed along the west coast of southern India. These have generally been considered to be related to the Deccan basalts. However, neither reliable palaeomagnetic directions nor precise radiomet- [uc] ric ages have been available for these dykes. Similarly, although many conventional K-Ar iso- tope ages have been reported for Deccan rocks, the duration of Deccan volcanism has been un- certain [1], and relationships between the dykes and Deccan volcanism have not been properly evaluated. ke swarms occurring within the granulite terrain in central Kerala (west coast of India). Palaeomagnetic data show that the NNW-SSE leucogabbro dykes sampled are normally magnetised (D = 307 and I = -57), whereas most NW-SE dolerite dykes are reversely magnetised (D = 163 and I = 61). One dolerite dyke shows normal polarity. The present 4°Ar/39Ar isotope ages for dolerite dykes and previously reported K-Ar ages for leucogabbros suggest 81 + 2 Ma for acquisition of the leucogabbro directions and 69 + 1 Ma for acquisition of the reverse magnetic directions within the dolerites. Based on palaeomagnetic and isotopic age data, the dolerite dykes appears to represent feeder systems for the Deccan volcanic sequences. We suggest that the Deccan eruptions were widespread, and probably extended southward at least into central Kerala. The entire magmatic episode may have occurred between ca. 70 and 65 Ma (during the 31R period probably corresponding to the Cretaceous/Tertiary boundary). The leucogabbros may correspond to the 34N superchron and represent a plume-related magmatic episode precursory to the main volcanic event. These data suggest that an early intraplate plume tectonic setting (since ca. 80 Ma) preceded lithospheric thinning, asthenospheric upwelling and consequent mas

The leucogabbros may correspond to the 34N superchron and represent a plume-related magmatic episode precursory to the main volcanic event. These data suggest that an early intraplate plume tectonic setting (since ca. 80 Ma) preceded lithospheric thinning, asthenospheric upwelling and consequent massive flood volcanism during the period 70-65 Ma. This culminated in ocean-floor spreading between the Seychelles-Mascarene and continental India. I. Introduction Several Phanerozoic dyke swarms are exposed along the west coast of southern India. These have generally been considered to be related to the Deccan basalts. However, neither reliable palaeomagnetic directions nor precise radiomet- [uc] ric ages have been available for these dykes. Similarly, although many conventional K-Ar iso- tope ages have been reported for Deccan rocks, the duration of Deccan volcanism has been un- certain [1], and relationships between the dykes and Deccan volcanism have not been properly evaluated. section_candidates.excerpt: ELSEVIER Earth and Planetary Science Letters 121 (1994) 503-518 EPSL Counterclockwise rotation of Northeast Japan: Paleomagnetic evidence for regional extent and timing of rotation Yo-ichiro Otofuji a, Ayumi Kambara a, Takaaki Matsuda b, Susumu Nohda ¢ a Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Faculty of Science, Kobe University, Kobe 657, Japan b Department of Geology, Faculty of Science, Himeji Institute of Technology, Himeji 671-22, Japan c Kyoto Sangyo University, Kamigamo, Kita-ku, Kyoto 603, Japan (Received August 19, 1993; revision accepted November 25, 1993) Abstract Early to Late Miocene welded tufts have been sampled from northeast Honshu Island and the Oshima Peninsula of Hokkaido Island, Japan for paleomagnetic study. Characteristic directions with a high unblocking temperature component above 560°C are isolated from 24 sites. Westerly declinations (D = - 1 ° ~ - 91 °) are identified in welded tufts older than 17 Ma from these areas. When combined with previous paleomagnetic data from welded tufts, the Early Miocene paleomagnetic poles derived from northeast Honshu Island and the Oshima Peninsula are statisti- cally identical and indicate that northeast Honshu Island and the Oshima Peninsula were subjected to counterclock- wise rotation as a sin

rotating block of Northeast Japan extends north to the Oshima Peninsula to the latitude 43°N. The dimension of this rotating block is of the order of 500 kin. The paleomagnetic data provide a best curve for the rotation process, with the counterclockwise rotation reaching a climax at 15.0 Ma and a net amount of rotation of 46.4 °. The 500 km long Northeast Japan block was rotated counterclockwise through more than 45 ° and accompanied a clockwise rotation of the 600 km long Southwest Japan block at about 15 Ma. 1. Introduction Peripheral parts of the continental crust typi- cally behave as a non-rigid assemblage associated with the formation of back-arc basins. As a con- sequence continental material is often split into blocks which separate from the mother continent [1]. A typical example is observed in the Japan arc and Sea of Japan system (Fig. 1). From the [UCl evidence of recent paleomagnetic studies along the Japan arc and ODP results from the Japan Sea [2-6], continental blocks forming the Japan arc are interpreted to have drifted and rotated as a consequence of the opening of the Sea of Japan between 25 and 12 Ma. A number of models have been proposed for the rifting process on the basis of geological and geophysical data derived from the Sea of Japan area

These two blocks are con- sidered to have experienced differential rotation when the Sea of Japan was opened. The regional extent of the rigid block compris- ing SW Japan during this clockwise rotational motion has been clearly established. Itoh and Ito [8] show from paleomagnetic evidence that the area from Kyushu to Fukui behaved as an intact block during the rotation. The le

geological observations suggest that the rigid area of NE Japan ranges from the Kanto district to the west- ern part of Hokkaido Island (see Fig. 1 and [1,9-12]), most paleomagnetic studies have sug- gested that only northeast Honshu Island was rotated counterclockwise as an intact block [2,13- 15]. Kawai et al. [15] note the possibility of rela- tive rotation between the western part of Hokkaido Island and northeast Honshu Island. These controversies relate to the lack of paleo- magnetic data from the northern part of Honshu Island and the western part of Hokkaido Island. As a step toward resolving this issue we have collected samples from the Yamagata area on Honshu Island to the western part of Hokkaido Island (Fig. 1). The primary subject of our paleo- magnetic study is the Oligocene to Late Miocene welded tuffs. These are highlighted because the rotational motion of NE Japan occurred during this period [2,14,16] and because welded tuffs have been shown to provide reliable magnetiza- tions and radiometric ages. 2. Characteristic directions with a high unblocking temperature component above 560°C are isolated from 24 sites. Westerly declinations (D = - 1 ° ~ - 91 °) are identified in welded tufts older than 17 Ma from these areas. rotating block of Northeast Japan extends north to the Oshima Peninsula to the latitude 43°N. The dimension of this rotating block is of the order of 500 kin. The paleomagnetic data provide a best curve for the rotation process, with the counterclockwise rotation reaching a climax at 15.0 Ma and a net amount of rotation of 46.4 °. The 500 km long Northeast Japan block was rotated counterclockwise through more than 45 ° and accompanied a clockwise rotation of the 600 km long Southwest Japan block at about 15 Ma. 1. Introduction Peripheral parts of the continental crust typi- cally behave as a non-rigid assemblage associated with the formation of back-arc basins. As a con- sequence continental material is often split into blocks which separate from the mother continent [1]. A typical example is observed in the Japan arc and Sea of Japan system (Fig. 1). From the [UCl evidence of recent paleomagnetic studies along the Japan arc and ODP results from the Japan Sea [2-6], continental blocks forming the Japan arc are interpreted to have drifted and rotated as a consequence of the opening of the Sea of Japan between 25 and 12 Ma. A number of models have been proposed for the rifting process on the basis of geological and geophysical data derived from the Sea of Japan area

The regional extent of the rigid block compris- ing SW Japan during this clockwise rotational motion has been clearly established. geological observations suggest that the rigid area of NE Japan ranges from the Kanto district to the west- ern part of Hokkaido Island (see Fig. 1 and [1,9-12]), most paleomagnetic studies have sug- gested that only northeast Honshu Island was rotated counterclockwise as an intact block [2,13- 15]. Kawai et al. [15] note the possibility of rela- tive rotation between the western part of Hokkaido Island and northeast Honshu Island. These controversies relate to the lack of paleo- magnetic data from the northern part of Honshu Island and the western part of Hokkaido Island. Characteristic directions with a high unblocking temperature component above 560°C are isolated from 24 sites. Westerly declinations (D = - 1 ° ~ - 91 °) are identified in welded tufts older than 17 Ma from these areas. When combined with previous paleomagnetic data from welded tufts, the Early Miocene paleomagnetic poles derived from northeast Honshu Island and the Oshima Peninsula are statisti- cally identical and indicate that northeast Honshu Island and the Oshima Peninsula were subjected to counterclock- wise rotation as a sin

rotating block of Northeast Japan extends north to the Oshima Peninsula to the latitude 43°N. The dimension of this rotating block is of the order of 500 kin. The paleomagnetic data provide a best curve for the rotation process, with the counterclockwise rotation reaching a climax at 15.0 Ma and a net amount of rotation of 46.4 °. The 500 km long Northeast Japan block was rotated counterclockwise through more than 45 ° and accompanied a clockwise rotation of the 600 km long Southwest Japan block at about 15 Ma. 1. Introduction Peripheral parts of the continental crust typi- cally behave as a non-rigid assemblage associated with the formation of back-arc basins. As a con- sequence continental material is often split into blocks which separate from the mother continent [1]. A typical example is observed in the Japan arc and Sea of Japan system (Fig. 1). From the [UCl evidence of recent paleomagnetic studies along the Japan arc and ODP results from the Japan Sea [2-6], continental blocks forming the Japan arc are interpreted to have drifted and rotated as a consequence of the opening of the Sea of Japan between 25 and 12 Ma. A number of models have been proposed for the rifting process on the basis of geological and geophysical data derived from the Sea of Japan area

The regional extent of the rigid block compris- ing SW Japan during this clockwise rotational motion has been clearly established. Itoh and Ito [8] show from paleomagnetic evidence that the area from Kyushu to Fukui behaved as an intact block during the rotation. The le

geological observations suggest that the rigid area of NE Japan ranges from the Kanto district to the west- ern part of Hokkaido Island (see Fig. 1 and [1,9-12]), most paleomagnetic studies have sug- gested that only northeast Honshu Island was rotated counterclockwise as an intact block [2,13- 15]. Kawai et al. [15] note the possibility of rela- tive rotation between the western part of Hokkaido Island and northeast Honshu Island. These controversies relate to the lack of paleo- magnetic data from the northern part of Honshu Island and the western part of Hokkaido Island. Geological setting and sampling The Lesser Kuril Islands and the the Nemuro Peninsula in the easternmost part of Hokkaido are an area without present-day volcanic activity on the Pacific side of the Kuril island arc (Fig. 1). About 340 cores from 43 sites of Lower Cretaceous red beds were sampled from four different localities in the basin and adjacent ranges. A well-defined component of magnetization (A) of normal polarity with high unblocking temperatures up to 650-670°C was isolated from all the sites. Another component of magnetization (B) with unblocking temperatures between 650 and 680°C was isolated from only fifteen sites; this component is bipolar. The fold test is positive for both components. We believe that component A was acquired during the Cretaceous long interval of normal polarity. Introduction Fold belt formation is commonly attributed to collision of lithospheric plates. The Alpine belt is thought to have resulted from Cenozoic collision -of the African plate, in the west, and the Indian plate, in the east, with the Eurasia landmass. Indentation of Eurasia by the rigid Indian wed

l debatable, in particular the magnitude of horizontal movements and associ- ated rotations. Paleomagnetic data may be of great impor- tance in elucidating this problem, and indeed the Cretaceous and Paleogene rocks of the Tadzhik depression, the southern part of the Tien Shan (the Ghissar range) and the westernmost Pamirs have already been studied. The main body of data from the depression and the Ghissar range, however, is based on time-cleaning techniques only [e.g., 31 and thus cannot be considered. reli- able. In addition, a result from the western bor- der of the Pamirs based on thermal cleaning up to 400°C and a positive fold test [4] is also not of top quality compared to modern standards. Re- cently, Pozzi and Feinberg [5] presented fully demagnetized data from the northeast Tadzhik basin, but from a limited number of samples. To study the main features of the Alpine tec- tonics in both the Tien Shan and Tadzhik depres- sions, structural and paleomagnetic studies were carried out by French-Soviet expeditions in Kirghizia and Tadzhikistan during the 1989-1990 field seasons. In Tadzhikistan, both Oligocene- Lower Miocene and Lower Cretaceous rocks were sampled at a number of localities. This paper covers the results of the Cretaceous collection. 2. Geolo

Introduction Fold belt formation is commonly attributed to collision of lithospheric plates. The Alpine belt is thought to have resulted from Cenozoic collision -of the African plate, in the west, and the Indian plate, in the east, with the Eurasia landmass. Indentation of Eurasia by the rigid Indian wed

l debatable, in particular the magnitude of horizontal movements and associ- ated rotations. Paleomagnetic data may be of great impor- tance in elucidating this problem, and indeed the Cretaceous and Paleogene rocks of the Tadzhik depression, the southern part of the Tien Shan (the Ghissar range) and the westernmost Pamirs have already been studied. The main body of data from the depression and the Ghissar range, however, is based on time-cleaning techniques only [e.g., 31 and thus cannot be considered. reli- able. In addition, a result from the western bor- der of the Pamirs based on thermal cleaning up to 400°C and a positive fold test [4] is also not of top quality compared to modern standards. Re- cently, Pozzi and Feinberg [5] presented fully demagnetized data from the northeast Tadzhik basin, but from a limited number of samples. To study the main features of the Alpine tec- tonics in both the Tien Shan and Tadzhik depres- sions, structural and paleomagnetic studies were carried out by French-Soviet expeditions in Kirghizia and Tadzhikistan during the 1989-1990 field seasons. Introduction Fold belt formation is commonly attributed to collision of lithospheric plates. The Alpine belt is thought to have resulted from Cenozoic collision -of the African plate, in the west, and the Indian plate, in the east, with the Eurasia landmass. Indentation of Eurasia by the rigid Indian wed

l debatable, in particular the magnitude of horizontal movements and associ- ated rotations. Paleomagnetic data may be of great impor- tance in elucidating this problem, and indeed the Cretaceous and Paleogene rocks of the Tadzhik depression, the southern part of the Tien Shan (the Ghissar range) and the westernmost Pamirs have already been studied. The main body of data from the depression and the Ghissar range, however, is based on time-cleaning techniques only [e.g., 31 and thus cannot be considered. reli- able. In addition, a result from the western bor- der of the Pamirs based on thermal cleaning up to 400°C and a positive fold test [4] is also not of top quality compared to modern standards. Re- cently, Pozzi and Feinberg [5] presented fully demagnetized data from the northeast Tadzhik basin, but from a limited number of samples. About 340 cores from 43 sites of Lower Cretaceous red beds were sampled from four different localities in the basin and adjacent ranges. A well-defined component of magnetization (A) of normal polarity with high unblocking temperatures up to 650-670°C was isolated from all the sites. Another component of magnetization (B) with unblocking temperatures between 650 and 680°C was isolated from only fifteen sites; this component is bipolar. The fold test is positive for both components. We believe that component A was acquired during the Cretaceous long interval of normal polarity. Introduction Fold belt formation is commonly attributed to collision of lithospheric plates. The Alpine belt is thought to have resulted from Cenozoic collision -of the African plate, in the west, and the Indian plate, in the east, with the Eurasia landmass. Indentation of Eurasia by the rigid Indian wed

l debatable, in particular the magnitude of horizontal movements and associ- ated rotations. Paleomagnetic data may be of great impor- tance in elucidating this problem, and indeed the Cretaceous and Paleogene rocks of the Tadzhik depression, the southern part of the Tien Shan (the Ghissar range) and the westernmost Pamirs have already been studied. The main body of data from the depression and the Ghissar range, however, is based on time-cleaning techniques only [e.g., 31 and thus cannot be considered. reli- able. Indentation of Eurasia by the rigid Indian wed

Paleomagnetic data may be of great impor- tance in elucidating this problem, and indeed the Cretaceous and Paleogene rocks of the Tadzhik depression, the southern part of the Tien Shan (the Ghissar range) and the westernmost Pamirs have already been studied. The paleomagnetic behavior of the sequence of floodplain paleosols of varying degrees of maturation ranges from excellent to poor. We present a magnetostratigraphic section for a composite section near Worland, Wyoming, by using a set of strict criteria for interpreting the step-wise alternating field and thermal demagnetization data of 266 samples from 90 sites throughout the composite section. Our correlation suggests that the Bighorn Basin composite section in the Worland area spans from within Chron C24r to near the top of Chron C24n, or from approximately 55 to 52 Ma. Correlation to the geomagnetic reversal time scale was achieved by combining magnetostratigraphic and biostratigraphic data from this section, from a section in the Clark's Fork Basin in northern Wyoming, and from DSDP Site 550, with the isotopic date determined on a tuff near the top of our section. Our correlation suggests that the Bighorn Basin composite section in the Worland area spans from within Chron C24r to near the top of Chron C24n, or from approximately 55 to 52 Ma. This correlation places the Paleocene/Eocene boundary within the vicinity of the base of the section. Cryptochron C24r.6 of Cande and Kent is tentative

on a tuff near the top of our section. Our correlation suggests that the Bighorn Basin composite section in the Worland area spans from within Chron C24r to near the top of Chron C24n, or from approximately 55 to 52 Ma. This correlation places the Paleocene/Eocene boundary within the vicinity of the base of the section. Cryptochron C24r.6 of Cande and Kent is tentatively identified some 100 m above the base of the section. It also provides independent chronological information for the calculation of sediment accumulation rates to constrain soil maturation rates. We exclude an age as young as 53 Ma for the Paleocene/Eocene boundary and support older ages, as recommended in recent time scales. Primary thermoremanence has been demonstrated in samples from 23 sites in a tilted Cretaceous-Palaeogene lava sequence in the Balantak ophiolite at Batusimpang on the eastern tip of the East Arm of Sulawesi. Its direction (D = 60.5 °, I = -32.1 °, a95 = 5.5 °) indicates formation at 17 + 4°S and ~ 60 ° of subsequent clockwise rotation. The primary mode of remanence is deduced from NRM/TRM comparisons; low-temperature cycling and other rock magnetic tests point to SD magnetite as the principal remanence carrier. Supporting evidence for the palaeolatitude and northward movement of the East Arm is derived from other lavas at Binsil, and from the Boba Cherts, but lack of tectonic control limits the interpretation. The contrast between these results and the subequatorial origin of contemporary rocks on nearly Halmahera is consistent with subduction of Indian Ocean lithosphere beneath the Sunda margin in the late Mesozoic and early Tertiary. Large differences in declination of remanence in the E Sulawesi rocks indicate large clockwise and anticlockwise rotations of tectonic blocks only tens of kilometres across.

In some areas there is a transition to the sheeted complex. On the coast of the East Arm there is a faulted contact between sheeted dykes and basalts. The lavas are highly faulted and it is difficult to deter- mine their thickness; if there is no repetition there may be up to 3 km of lavas in places. Most of the basalts are porphyritic with phenocrysts of plagioclase and pyroxene in a glassy matrix con- taining microlites of plagioclase, pyroxene and magnetite and they commonly contain amygdales up to 2.5 cm across, filled by zeolites and/or calcite. The basalts are typically highly altered with plagioclase replaced by zeolites, saussurite and carbonate; pyroxene is replaced by chlorite, epidote, iron oxides and rarely hornblende; olivine is altered to serpentine; and glass is partially devitrified. In parts of the East Arm sedimentary rocks are tectonically associated with ophiolitic rocks. Introduction The tectonically active regions between Asia and Australia are of general geological interest because they are the site of perhaps the most spectacular convergence and accretion of crust that is currently occurring anywhere on Earth. An understanding of the present-day geology and tectonics together with the unravelling of their development over the last 100 m.y. constitute a model scenario that should throw light on the [RvdV] evolution of older plate convergence zones. The region is large and immensely complex and the evidence is both fragmentary and obscure, and hence the whole range of available geoscientific techniques needs to be used in order to recon- struct its history. Geological evidence indicates that fragments in the tectonic mosaic

orded by Late Miocene volcanic rocks of the Southwest Arm are indistinguishable from those of Earth's present magnetic field. The palaeo- magnetic results from SW Sulawesi are very simi- lar to those from Cretaceous rocks of the Malay Peninsula [7] and Borneo [8], suggesting little latitudinal movement between these areas and similar anticlockwise rotations since the Late Mesozoic and before the Late Miocene. Otofuji et al. [9] suggested that the North Arm of Su- lawesi has rotated clockwise by more than 90 ° with no significant latitude change since the Eocene-Early Miocene, but their data are insuf- ficient to justify any such conclusion. ODP Leg 124 drilling in the Celebes Sea indicated no sig- nificant difference from present-day latitude, but about a 60 ° anticlockwise rotation between the late Eocene and Early Miocene. 3. Primary thermoremanence has been demonstrated in samples from 23 sites in a tilted Cretaceous-Palaeogene lava sequence in the Balantak ophiolite at Batusimpang on the eastern tip of the East Arm of Sulawesi. Its direction (D = 60.5 °, I = -32.1 °, a95 = 5.5 °) indicates formation at 17 + 4°S and ~ 60 ° of subsequent clockwise rotation. The primary mode of remanence is deduced from NRM/TRM comparisons; low-temperature cycling and other rock magnetic tests point to SD magnetite as the principal remanence carrier. Supporting evidence for the palaeolatitude and northward movement of the East Arm is derived from other lavas at Binsil, and from the Boba Cherts, but lack of tectonic control limits the interpretation. Large differences in declination of remanence in the E Sulawesi rocks indicate large clockwise and anticlockwise rotations of tectonic blocks only tens of kilometres across.

In some areas there is a transition to the sheeted complex. On the coast of the East Arm there is a faulted contact between sheeted dykes and basalts. The lavas are highly faulted and it is difficult to deter- mine their thickness; if there is no repetition there may be up to 3 km of lavas in places. Most of the basalts are porphyritic with phenocrysts of plagioclase and pyroxene in a glassy matrix con- taining microlites of plagioclase, pyroxene and magnetite and they commonly contain amygdales up to 2.5 cm across, filled by zeolites and/or calcite. The basalts are typically highly altered with plagioclase replaced by zeolites, saussurite and carbonate; pyroxene is replaced by chlorite, epidote, iron oxides and rarely hornblende; olivine is altered to serpentine; and glass is partially devitrified. In parts of the East Arm sedimentary rocks are tectonically associated with ophiolitic rocks. There is locally calcilutite infilling of pillow interstices and in some areas lavas or hyalo- clastites are overlain by lenticular calcilutites; all are unfossiliferous. In the Boba River, cherts

Introduction The tectonically active regions between Asia and Australia are of general geological interest because they are the site of perhaps the most spectacular convergence and accretion of crust that is currently occurring anywhere on Earth. An understanding of the present-day geology and tectonics together with the unravelling of their development over the last 100 m.y. constitute a model scenario that should throw light on the [RvdV] evolution of older plate convergence zones. The region is large and immensely complex and the evidence is both fragmentary and obscure, and hence the whole range of available geoscientific techniques needs to be used in order to recon- struct its history. Geological evidence indicates that fragments in the tectonic mosaic

orded by Late Miocene volcanic rocks of the Southwest Arm are indistinguishable from those of Earth's present magnetic field. The palaeo- magnetic results from SW Sulawesi are very simi- lar to those from Cretaceous rocks of the Malay Peninsula [7] and Borneo [8], suggesting little latitudinal movement between these areas and similar anticlockwise rotations since the Late Mesozoic and before the Late Miocene. Otofuji et al. [9] suggested that the North Arm of Su- lawesi has rotated clockwise by more than 90 ° with no significant latitude change since the Eocene-Early Miocene, but their data are insuf- ficient to justify any such conclusion. ODP Leg 124 drilling in the Celebes Sea indicated no sig- nificant difference from present-day latitude, but about a 60 ° anticlockwise rotation between the late Eocene and Early Miocene. 3. In some areas there is a transition to the sheeted complex. On the coast of the East Arm there is a faulted contact between sheeted dykes and basalts. The lavas are highly faulted and it is difficult to deter- mine their thickness; if there is no repetition there may be up to 3 km of lavas in places. Most of the basalts are porphyritic with phenocrysts of plagioclase and pyroxene in a glassy matrix con- taining microlites of plagioclase, pyroxene and magnetite and they commonly contain amygdales up to 2.5 cm across, filled by zeolites and/or calcite. Introduction The tectonically active regions between Asia and Australia are of general geological interest because they are the site of perhaps the most spectacular convergence and accretion of crust that is currently occurring anywhere on Earth. An understanding of the present-day geology and tectonics together with the unravelling of their development over the last 100 m.y. constitute a model scenario that should throw light on the [RvdV] evolution of older plate convergence zones. The region is large and immensely complex and the evidence is both fragmentary and obscure, and hence the whole range of available geoscientific techniques needs to be used in order to recon- struct its history. Geological evidence indicates that fragments in the tectonic mosaic

e western volcanic arc [e.g., 1-4], resulting in ophiolite emplacement and metamorphism. How- ever, as work in the region has progressed it has become clear that this apparent simplicity is partly a reflection of the incomplete knowledge of a large area which is remote, mountainous and largely covered by thick rainforest. In particular, little is known of the age and origin of the East Sulawesi ophiolite, which is likely to have formed far from its present position. 2. Previous palaeomagnetic work There has been little previous palaeomagnetic work on Sulawesi. The earliest results were re- ported by Haile [5] from oriented block samples of cherts from the Southwest and Southeast Arms. They indicated that these arms were situated in different palaeogeographic regions during the Late Jurassic-Early Cretaceous, as proposed by Audley-Charles et al. [2] and Katili [3]. Data from SW Sulawesi indicate that the Southwest Arm has remained close to its present latitude since the Late Jurassic [5] and late Paleogene [6] but has rotated anticlockwise by about 45 °. Directions recorded by Late Miocene volcanic rocks of the Southwest Arm are indistinguishable from those of Earth's present magnetic field. Thus the magnetization must be coeval with or later than mineralization. Combined with the two negative breccia tests and epigenetic paragenetic sequence, the magnetization must postdate the mid-Mississippian host rocks. Scotese et al. [1984] reported a positive palcomagnetic fold test on rocks from several horizons nearby in the Windsor Group, indicating a pre-Alleghenian orogeny or pre-late Pennsylvanian magnetization. Our fold test is inconclusive, but our samples show similar ChRM characteristics to those found by Scotese et al. [1984] except for a 14 ø difference in declina- tion. Most of our sites are near the mine whereas those of Scotese et al. [1984] are much further away, so that the discord- ante could be caused by rotations on known postore faults near the mine. Geology Basement rocks at Gays River (Fig. 1), between the Schubenacadie' and Musquodoboit basins, consist of folded greenschist facies metasediments of the Cambro-Ordovician Megurea Group into which Devonian gtanitoid plutons were eraplaced during the Acadian orogeny [Keppie, 1982]. Alteration and mineralization of dolostones in the Gays River Formation of the Windsor Group took place without a volume change, preserving primary porosity and fossil structures [Schenk, 1984]. A basal breccia of a near-sedimentary karstic origin has fragments up to several meters across [Schenk, 1984].
